chapter: San Francisco, the So Different Orchestra and Johnny
title: Union examination, Thornburgh and the San Francisco musicians' strike
summary: The Musicians Union kept the band from the Portola job because several players could not read; Thornburgh sent them to Los Angeles and later brought them back during a strike.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Well, anyway, when Old Man Thornburgh who owned the place come down and hired us to play, the Union kicked because we weren't Union people. They didn't want us to go in there, so we had to go and take a musical examination at the Union, and they said I could read, and the saxophone could read...I mean I could read and the clarinet player could read and the flute player could read but the piano player and the drummer and the bass player couldn't read, so they all...in other words, they split up our band. We

couldn't have no band. They... We couldn't get the job, but Old Man Thornburgh then sent us down here to Los Angeles, his friend which was Al Levy that owned the Watts Country Club then, you know, called Levy's Tavern, and after we was down here five or six weeks, the musicians struck in San Francisco, had a big musicians' strike, and Old Man Thornburgh come down here and got us and took us back to San Francisco. 'Course, you could always get a white band, you know, so it was easy to go up and get a white band to fill in our place but you couldn't get a colored band good like that so he come down here, and they released us. The only reason he let us come down here was because the Union said we couldn't read up there. So we went back up there, and when we went back up there and went to work, the white Union used to parade out in front and tell them to stay out of there 'cause they had a bunch of Negro boys in there and they couldn't read and were scabs and didn't belong to the Union and nothing else, and they said that...uh...that went on for a long time till it died out. It didn't stop anybody from coming. The crowds got bigger and bigger 'cause they used to have to lock the door to keep them out 'cause they'd never heard a colored band like that, you know, and we were... this boy Mitchell--Slocum, I called him--he was one of them weird clarinet players like a saxophone on the trumpet. See, he started all that stuff.
